assessment.nobel_worthiness: A clean, universal mechanism: spin-orbit coupling plus time-reversal symmetry yields a Z2 topological invariant and protected edge or surface states. It began as a simple tight-binding model on graphene, was generalised to three dimensions, and reshaped how bands and materials are classified. The idea is simple, general and rigorously analysable, and it extends the 2016 prize on topological phases without duplicating it.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall idea; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposed HgTe wells, and Molenkamp's group observed the edge transport in 2007. The 3D materials (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy; Hasan's ARPES on Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3) are a further strand. Three names cannot cover everyone. I would take the two theorists and the first decisive experiment, noting that Hasan is a defensible alternative for the 3D materials.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The quantum spin Hall and 3D topological insulator results have been reproduced by many groups for about 15 years and are textbook material. The recognition is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Credit is split between the 2D and 3D theory and several experimental groups; a three-person slate leaves out the defensible contributor Hasan.
Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu, Moore and Balents are not among the supplied credited names, and I cannot independently verify the precise priority claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-angle prediction (a flat band from moire interference), followed by the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, opened a field. It gives a tunable platform for studying strong correlation directly, and a simple continuum model made a precise, testable prediction.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald gave the continuum-model magic-angle prediction (2011). Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery. Andrei's group made early independent experimental contributions. The three-person slate fits the theory-plus-experiment pattern.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature: many independent reproductions and a large follow-on literature. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated and the field is moving fast, so recognition may be slightly early.
uncertainties: The origin of the superconducting pairing is unresolved.
Andrei's early experimental work and other groups raise a credit question that three names cannot fully settle.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems and the Jarzynski equality are exact results valid arbitrarily far from equilibrium, extending the second law to small systems. They are conceptually fundamental and have been tested in single-molecule and colloidal experiments. This is statistical physics of the kind I value: exact, general and understood.
assessment.attribution: Evans, Cohen and Morriss (1993) and Gallavotti-Cohen (1995) gave the first fluctuation theorems, Jarzynski (1997) the work relation, and Crooks (1999) the detailed relation. The credit chain is real but the supplied names omit Cohen, Morriss and Gallavotti. I favour Jarzynski and Evans, and Crooks is a defensible third.
assessment.maturity: Mature in theory and well tested experimentally (RNA pulling, optical traps, nanoscale electronics). Its effect on practice, for example in free-energy computation, is clear.
uncertainties: The priority question among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Gallavotti and Jarzynski is unresolved and incompletely represented in the credited names.
It may be judged more as a theorem than a physical discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Inflation explains flatness, horizon uniformity and the origin of primordial fluctuations, and the quantum-origin-of-structure calculation is a clean statistical argument giving a quantitative spectrum that matches the CMB. It is among the most consequential ideas in modern cosmology.
assessment.attribution: Guth proposed inflation, Linde (new and chaotic inflation) and Albrecht-Steinhardt repaired it, Starobinsky had an earlier model, and Mukhanov-Chibisov and others computed the fluctuation spectrum. Starobinsky is not among the supplied names, so any slate is incomplete and contentious.
assessment.maturity: The CMB spectrum (WMAP, Planck) supports the generic predictions, but there is no direct evidence of inflation itself (for example primordial B-modes) and alternatives are not fully excluded. Possibly premature as a prize for the mechanism.
uncertainties: No direct detection of primordial gravitational waves; the mechanism is inferred.
Starobinsky and others are missing from the credited names, so the allocation is disputed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fractional statistics in two dimensions is a deep idea: particle exchange can give phases other than plus or minus one. The 1977 Leinaas-Myrheim paper and its later realisation in the fractional quantum Hall regime (fractional charge, then interferometric and collision evidence for anyons) link a topological idea to observation.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim introduced anyonic statistics; Wilczek named and developed it, which the supplied names do not cover. Heiblum measured fractional charge in shot noise and later experiments, with Fève and Manfra on the anyon-braiding side. Charge and statistics might need separate recognition.
assessment.maturity: Moderate. Fractional charge is well established, while anyon braiding and collision signatures have appeared only in recent years in a few groups and some interpretations are still discussed. The 1998 prize already covered the fractional quantum Hall effect itself.
uncertainties: Wilczek is not in the credited names, which leaves the theoretical credit incomplete.
Independent confirmation of anyonic braiding is recent and rests on a small number of groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The KTHNY theory of two-dimensional melting by dislocation and disclination unbinding, with an intermediate hexatic phase, is a good example of a simple, universal mechanism with quantitative predictions. It extends the topological-defect idea behind the 2016 prize and has been tested in colloids and other systems.
assessment.attribution: Halperin and Nelson, and independently Young, developed the dislocation-mediated theory building on Kosterlitz and Thouless, who were already honoured. Credit among these three is reasonably clear.
assessment.maturity: The theory dates from 1978-79 and has been probed in colloidal and other experiments, although simulations show that the melting scenario depends on the system (first-order transitions occur). Mature, with some residual system dependence.
uncertainties: The melting scenario varies between systems and some are first-order, so the universality is partial.
It may be seen as an extension of already awarded work and therefore lower in novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The funnelled energy landscape and minimal-frustration principle explain how heteropolymers fold quickly, borrowing spin-glass and random-energy-model methods. It is understanding, not only prediction, of a complex system, and it has influenced biophysics and structure-prediction methods.
assessment.attribution: Bryngelson and Wolynes (1987) brought spin-glass ideas to folding, and Onuchic, Luthey-Schulten and Wolynes developed the funnel picture. Dill's work on hydrophobic collapse and lattice models is parallel. Bryngelson is not among the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: The concept is widely accepted, but it is a framework rather than a single decisive confirmation, and the 2024 chemistry prize for protein structure prediction and design changes the context. The physics versus chemistry boundary is a risk.
uncertainties: Discipline fit (physics versus chemistry) and its framework character make the discovery harder to define.
Credit among Wolynes, Onuchic, Dill and Bryngelson is not cleanly settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a non-perturbative treatment of strongly correlated electrons, exact in infinite dimensions. It describes the Mott transition and underlies modern computational methods for correlated materials (DFT+DMFT). The method is clear, widely used and has a rigorous limit.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt (1989) introduced the infinite-dimension limit, and Georges and Kotliar (1992) mapped it to an impurity problem. Muller-Hartmann and Jarrell also contributed. Metzner is not in the supplied names, which makes the allocation questionable.
assessment.maturity: Mature: three decades of use, with extensions to clusters and to realistic materials. It is an approximation in finite dimension, so the discovery is less sharp than a new phenomenon.
uncertainties: It is a theoretical method rather than the discovery of a phenomenon, which may weigh against it.
Metzner and Muller-Hartmann are missing from the credited names.
